This Week's Timetable

Trains start at Keighley, run up the Worth Valley to Oxenhope and back. Give each locomotive (and its carriage set) a list of departure times. Untick stations to make a train run through them without stopping, or untick the ends to make a shuttle (it must start and turn back at a loop, ⇄). The line is single track: trains can only pass at the loops at Damems and Haworth (and Oakworth, if you build one), so the signallers will hold one train at a loop until the other has cleared the single line.

Train workings

Train graph — time runs left to right, distance up the line from bottom to top. Flat lines are trains standing at a station; a long flat line at a loop is a train being held for a crossing.

Line Map

The Keighley & Worth Valley Railway: 4¾ miles of single line from the interchange with the Airedale Line at Keighley, up the valley of the River Worth through Ingrow Tunnel, past Oakworth, over Mytholmes Viaduct and through Mytholmes Tunnel to Haworth and the terminus at Oxenhope. The map is the real valley, from OpenStreetMap and the elevation survey. Click a station for details, and press play to watch the timetable run.

Events Calendar

Book galas, festivals and specials for future weekends. Book early: posters, adverts and the enthusiast press need about four weeks to spread the word, and an event booked at short notice draws a smaller crowd. A quarter of the cost is paid as a deposit when you book.

Haworth Shed

The railway's own locomotives and carriage sets. Keep condition healthy: a failure on the line strands passengers and blocks the single track.

Motive Power

Carriage Sets

Motive Power

Steam pulls the crowds but needs three crew and costs most to run. Heritage diesels are cheaper and reliable, and the diesel-gala crowd loves them. A diesel multiple unit needs no carriage set and turns round in minutes, but nobody travels specially to ride one.

Carriage Sets

A locomotive needs a rake. Longer sets carry more people but are harder work up the 1 in 56 out of Keighley: check the loco can haul it.

Works & Overhaul

A running repair is quick. A heavy overhaul restores a loco to as-new but takes it out of traffic for weeks: do them in winter. Every steam engine also needs a full overhaul once a year to renew its boiler ticket; the bigger the engine, the longer and dearer it is.

Volunteers & Upgrades

Like every heritage line, the Worth Valley runs on volunteers. Each operating day needs signallers and station staff, a crew for every train (three for steam, two for a diesel or DMU) and stewards for events. Busy weekends tire them out.

How to Play

You are general manager of the Keighley & Worth Valley Railway, the preserved branch line up the Worth Valley in West Yorkshire, from Keighley to Haworth and Oxenhope. Run normal services, organise steam and diesel galas, beer and music festivals, 1940s weekends and Santa specials, and grow the line until it's named Heritage Railway of the Year.

  • The laptop: each part of the railway is an app on the desktop. Double-click an icon (or tap it on a touch screen) to open its window; drag windows by the title bar, resize them from the corner, and switch between them on the taskbar. The Start button (the R&H roundel) lists every app.
  • Mail: railtour companies and other heritage railways email asking to hire your locomotives. Accept their offer, decline, or send a counter-offer: ask for more, but push too hard and they'll go elsewhere. A hired-out engine is away for the weeks agreed, and comes back a little more worn.
  • The yard: when you press Run the Weekend you can drive the Class 08 shunter yourself to make up the first train: the laptop folds away and you're in the cab. The yard is the loco yard at Haworth, in the old goods yard just beyond the platform. The coaches are already in the carriage siding; the train engine (and the pilot, for a double-header) is in the engine shed with the rest of the fleet, every engine facing the shunter. Set the points for the right shed road, buffer up to the engine, draw it out, set the points back to the carriage siding and buffer it up to the coaches, then uncouple. ↑/↓ (or W/S) drive, Space brakes, ←/→ (or A/D, or drag) look around, 1/2/3 set the points, U uncouples the shunter. Buffer up gently (under 2 mph) to couple. It's the same Haworth you drive through, so the shed you shunt in is the one you pass: engines not out that day stand in it, and engines in the works stand partly taken apart in the works extension beside it. Every class of engine is modelled from its own wheel arrangement, size and livery. Drive a service: or take a train out on the line yourself. Pick a train and the trip to start from, and drive it from the cab for the rest of its day, or just one way out or back, while the weekend runs on behind you (the other trains you meet are the weekend's own, and when you climb down the map carries on from the cab's clock): every booked call, the passing loops (the starter stays at danger until your time and a clear section), Ingrow Tunnel, Mytholmes Viaduct and Mytholmes Tunnel. The throttle (the regulator, on steam) and the brake are separate handles that stay where you leave them: W/S (or ↑/↓) open and close the throttle, E/D (or PgDn/PgUp) put the brake on and take it off, Space is the emergency brake, C changes the view (leaning out of the cab, sitting in the driver's seat behind the desk or the backhead, or from the lineside), T waits for the right away. Where the train turns back you run the engine round it: uncouple (U), draw forward over the points at that end of the loop and stop clear, set them for the loop (P), reverse (R) and run back along the loop past your coaches, set the far points for the loop before you run out over them, then set them back to the main line, reverse and buffer up gently to the other end of the coaches. Engines aren't turned, so trains come down from Oxenhope tender first (unless you have the Oxenhope turntable). Q (held) sounds the whistle or horn, M turns the sound off and on, H hands the train to another driver to finish the day. Every engine has its own synthesised sound: exhaust beats, diesel engines, whistles and horns. The line is the real Worth Valley, one to one: the track where it runs, the land from the elevation survey, and the valley's buildings, roads, drystone walls, woods, becks and reservoirs from OpenStreetMap. Each way takes about a quarter of an hour. If the timetable runs DMUs, you can drive each unit yourself from its own cab instead: out of the shed onto the headshunt, change ends (E), then into the carriage siding up to the STOP board. Or start in the shunter, climb down (F) and walk over to the unit (hold Shift or ⚡ Sprint to run). A clean, quick job lifts reputation and morale; or let the shed staff do it.
  • Each turn is one week. Plan the weekend in the Timetable app, then press Run the Weekend. Choose how many days to run: weekends, four days a week in the summer school holidays, or close for the week. The weekend then plays out live on the Line Map, all its days together in the time of one (change the speed there, or pause it). You can't start the next week until the last train is home, but you can carry on booking events, buying stock and recruiting while it runs. The takings arrive when the weekend ends.
  • Timetabling: every train is a round trip from Keighley to Oxenhope and back, about an hour with turn-rounds. Give each loco a set of departure times. If a train isn't back in time, its next trip leaves late.
  • The printed timetable: the Up and Down tables at the top of the Timetable app are the public timetable, a column for each train. The times are worked out by the signallers' plan, so a train held at a loop shows its real, later time. | means the train runs through without stopping.
  • Shuttles and non-stop trains: each train working has a row of stations it calls at. Untick a station in the middle and the train runs straight through it: quicker, but nobody can get on there. Untick the ends to make a shuttle, say Fellside–Oxenhope: it can only start and turn back at a passing loop (⇄), runs out empty from the shed in the morning and back at night, and its shorter rides sell cheaper tickets. Each station's passengers wait for a train that calls there; most people join at Keighley, where the car park is.
  • Liveries: every engine comes in a real livery its class carried, and can be repainted in any other it really wore: BR lined black, LNER apple green, LMS crimson lake, garter blue, BR blue, large logo, Railfreight, InterCity and more. Repaint in the Haworth Shed (volunteers, cheaper, two weeks) or at the Works (a contract paint shop, dearer, one week, with a lined works finish that draws a little more). Historic and famous liveries bring more visitors; the repaint window shows the engine in each one. DMUs can be repainted too, and visiting engines come in their owners' liveries. Running numbers: each engine you buy gets its own number from its class's real series (a pannier is a 57xx), painted on the cab side and the smokebox plate; repaint it into another era's livery and it is renumbered as it was then (41241 is 1241 in LMS black; a diesel carries its D number in green and its TOPS number in blue).
  • Double-heading: press 🚂🚂 Double-head on a diagram to couple a pilot engine on the front. The two engines' loads add together (a 4-coach and a 5-coach engine can take 9 coaches up the bank), so small engines can work long trains and climb faster. The crowd likes the sight, and a double-header counts as two engines for a gala, but it needs two crews, burns both engines' coal and wears both engines, and the train goes at the slower engine's pace.
  • Single line: trains can only pass at the loops (Damems and Haworth, plus Oakworth once built), and only one train may be on each single-line section. The train graph shows where trains are held. Each loop has one road for each direction (Oxenhope holds two trains), so too many trains with too few loops means trains are held and run late.
  • Passengers arrive through the day (mostly late morning and lunchtime) and take the next train. A gap of more than two hours loses them; a full train turns them away. Steam draws more people than diesel, and both draw more than a DMU.
  • Visiting stock: any event can bring visiting engines (up to 3) and visiting carriages (up to 2) on hire. As well as the star engines, every steam and diesel class in the shop can be hired on loan from another heritage line (a Black Five, a 37, a pannier...), each with its own number. For no gala at all, book Visiting Engine Running Days: ordinary running days with guests, on as many days as you like.
  • Saving: press 💾 Save / Load for a link containing the whole railway. Copy it, email it to yourself or download it as a file, then open it on any device (the Pi included) to carry on.
  • Events are booked on the calendar, ideally four weeks ahead. Galas need at least three engines of the right type in the timetable: hire guest engines when you book. Beer & music festivals fill the evening trains and the bar. Santa specials are the winter goldmine.
  • Volunteers crew every train. If a day needs more than turn up, you can't run it. Recruit, and keep morale up with a quiet week or a social.
  • Condition falls with every mile. Worn locos fail, and a failure blocks the line, refunds fares and costs reputation. Use the Works, and do heavy overhauls in winter.
  • Boiler tickets: a steam engine can only run while its boiler certificate is in date, and a certificate lasts a year. Renewing it means a full overhaul in the Works: a few weeks and a few thousand pounds for a small tank engine, three months and nearly £30,000 for a big tender engine like a Black Five or an 8F. The Fleet shows when each ticket runs out and you're warned 12 and 4 weeks ahead. Plan the overhauls for the winter so they're back for the season.
  • Seasons: spring and autumn are steady, summer is busy and the school holidays busiest of all; winter is dead apart from Santa specials. Weather matters too: check the forecast.
  • Goal: reach a net worth of £500,000 with a reputation of 110 or more. Finish two weeks in a row overdrawn and the railway closes.

An unofficial fan-made game, not connected with the Keighley & Worth Valley Railway. The line, the land and the buildings are the real valley's (map data © OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL; relief from the AWS Terrain Tiles); the people and companies who write to you are fictional.
